title: Weekly Deep Dive: AirBaltic's Bankruptcy and the A220's Reckoning
summary: AirBaltic just filed for Chapter 11, and it's not just a Latvian airline's problem — it's a stress test for the entire A220 program and the idea that betting your whole airline on one aircraft type is a smart strategy. Ryan and Hope dig into what actually broke at airBaltic, why the engines are the real villain of this story, and what it means for every other airline that's ordered hundreds of these jets.

topic.topic: AirBaltic's bankruptcy filing threatens the Airbus A220 business model and raises questions about airline viability when betting heavily on a single aircraft type.
topic.why: AirBaltic's Chapter 11 filing is the clearest signal yet that the A220 strategy—which was supposed to be transformational for regional airlines—carries existential risk. This isn't a routine restructuring; it's a fundamental challenge to one of aviation's biggest bets on aircraft commonality. The timing matters: the A220 is still ramping production, other carriers are doubling down on orders, and this failure could reshape the entire regional aviation ecosystem.
key_facts: AirBaltic, an all-Airbus operator with A220s central to its network, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection while claiming operations will continue
The A220 was pitched as the game-changer for regional profitability—lower costs, better range, higher margins than previous-generation regional jets
Multiple sources (Live and Let's Fly, Simple Flying, AirlineGeeks) covered the story on the same day, indicating broad industry recognition of significance
Airbus has aggressive A220 production targets and other carriers (Breeze, Air Canada, others) have ordered hundreds of these aircraft betting on similar unit economics
The filing raises questions about whether single-aircraft-type strategies are viable for carriers without massive scale or deep pockets

angles: Does the A220's unit economics actually work, or did AirBaltic simply execute poorly? What does this mean for other A220 operators who are counting on similar margins?
The concentration risk: What happens when you go all-in on a single aircraft type from a single manufacturer? How does this compare to carriers with mixed fleets?
Airbus's production ramp and customer confidence: With hundreds of A220s on order from other airlines, does AirBaltic's failure slow down the program or create buyer's remorse among customers?
